text: Open with the fan experience. CricketVerse is a capstone prototype that brings matchday fantasy, collectibles, polls, ticketing and contest participation into one product. Cover image is AI-generated for this presentation and is illustrative, not a photograph of a specific real match.
The project starts from a fan need: take part in the match and keep meaningful digital assets.
Stay connected to today’s match and its players.
Build a fantasy XI, vote and join a contest.
Collect player cards that belong to the fan’s wallet.
See rules for purchases, resale, entry and funds.
Motivation  ·  Put fan participation, ownership and rules in one connected experience.

This is the project motivation and design framing, not a claim that every existing cricket platform has the same shortcomings. Source basis: supplied CricketVerse project proposal and user-provided presentation materials.
Explore how a cricket app can connect live participation with user-owned assets and rules fans can inspect.
How can one platform connect matchday activity with digital ownership without putting fast-changing match data on-chain?
An integrated proof of concept combining a cricket-data API, a fan-facing web app and wallet-signed contract actions.
Describe this as an engineering and design contribution. No user study or measured impact is claimed in the current materials. Source basis: project proposal, app and server source.

The timeline is a user-facing summary of the features in the current app. Match and points availability depends on the cricket provider connection; purchases and other contract actions require a connected wallet. Source: public/app.js, server/server.js, BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md.
Matchday XI gives fans a role in the game
The app turns a confirmed playing list into a squad the fan can shape.

Role balance
Credit limit
Squad linked to contest entry
The cricket API supplies the match, playing XI and points; the app refreshes points as the provider updates them.

The code uses the provider playing XI as the available pool, validates an 11-player squad with role and credit constraints, and fetches match points from the API. Squad integrity is committed as a hash. Points are not currently validated by an on-chain oracle. Source: server/server.js, server/scoringEngine.js, public/app.js, BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md.

Blockchain records assets and enforces coded rules; it does not make a cricket score trustworthy by itself.

State the trust boundary precisely. The code has cricket API endpoints and contracts for assets and financial rules. Current deployment defaults to local Hardhat. The CricketOracleConsumer is not connected to a live Chainlink Functions subscription, and contest winners are selected by the organizer. Source: server/server.js, contracts/CricketOracleConsumer.sol, BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md.
Contracts matter when a fan needs ownership, a transaction record or a rule they can inspect.
Owned by a wallet; can be collected or traded
Used for demo purchases and contest entry
Resale limit and one-time redemption enforced by contract
Votes and entry funds recorded; prize settlement still needs an organizer
The 50,000 CRIC faucet is a local test feature, not a real-money reward.

The local CRIC contract gives test tokens through a wallet-signed faucet transaction. ERC-1155 cards and ERC-721 tickets are controlled by contracts. The marketplace escrows assets; tournament entries and refunds are on-chain, but the organizer settles winners. Source: contracts/CRIC.sol, PlayerCardNFT.sol, MatchTicketNFT.sol, CricketMarketplace.sol, TournamentPool.sol, FanPolls.sol, BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md.
The app joins cricket data to wallet actions
Two paths meet in the browser: one reads the match feed; the other asks the fan’s wallet to sign.
The current contract deployment is local to the developer’s computer.

This diagram summarises the implemented frontend/API/blockchain split. API endpoints rely on a provider key and network access. Browser wallet signs transactions, while contracts currently run on a local Hardhat network; other users cannot transact against this deployment from another computer. Source: public/app.js, public/chain.js, server/server.js, BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md.
Expected value should be tested with fans
These are outcomes to evaluate, not results claimed by the current prototype.
Can fans build an XI and manage a player card without help?
Can fans understand what is recorded on-chain and what comes from the API?
Can fans verify ticket rules, votes and contest-fund activity?
Evaluation focus  ·  task completion, rule correctness, data clarity and fan feedback.

These are proposed evaluation criteria, not measured outcomes. A future evaluation should test the fan journey with representative users, verify contract rules with automated tests, and report API failure and recovery behavior separately.

Current limitation  ·  tournament winners are reviewed and submitted by an organizer; live score data is not verified by a chain oracle.

Be explicit about prototype status. Current contracts-config.json targets Local Hardhat. BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md states that no public Amoy deployment or live Chainlink Functions subscription is configured, and tournament winners are organizer-selected. Provider routes exist but successful live data still depends on a configured key and provider availability. Source: BLOCKCHAIN_SETUP.md, server/server.js, public/contracts-config.json.
A practical evaluation can answer the research question
Assess both the fan experience and the correctness of the rules the prototype promises.
Ask fans to select an XI, find live points and collect a player card.
Test resale limits, one-time ticket redemption, escrow and refund paths.
Observe provider delay, missing fields, and recovery when the API is unavailable.
Report observed findings separately from intended impact.

This evaluation plan is a recommendation, not a description of completed user research. It separates usability, contract correctness and API reliability so one passing component does not imply the whole system is reliable.
Live cricket data keeps the experience current. Smart contracts make selected asset and transaction rules visible and enforceable.
A fan-centred prototype — with impact to be tested and trusted scoring still to be built.

Close with the main contribution and its boundary: the prototype combines a live-data experience with wallet-owned assets and contract-enforced rules, while fully trusted automated scoring remains future work.
